title: Module 6 Misconception Sort
intro: Decide whether each statement is true, false, or depends. These are the misconceptions that cost students points on exams.

items.s: A p value of .03 means there is a 3 percent chance the null hypothesis is true.
items.why: The p value is the probability of data this extreme if the null were true. It is not the probability that the null is true.

items.s: Failing to reject the null proves the null is true.
items.why: It means the data did not provide enough evidence against it. The study may have lacked power.

items.s: A statistically significant result is always a large or important effect.
items.why: With a big sample even a tiny effect can be significant. Effect size tells you how large it is.

items.s: Increasing the sample size increases power.
items.why: A larger n shrinks the standard error, so a real effect is easier to detect.

items.s: Making alpha smaller, such as .01 instead of .05, reduces the chance of a Type I error but raises the chance of a Type II error.
items.why: Stricter criteria make false alarms rarer and misses more likely.

items.s: The alternative hypothesis is proven when we reject the null.
items.why: Rejecting the null supports the alternative, but a single study does not prove anything.

items.s: Researchers should decide alpha after seeing the data.
items.why: Alpha is chosen in advance. Choosing it afterward inflates the Type I error rate.

items.s: A 95 percent confidence interval means 95 percent of individual scores lie inside it.
items.why: It describes plausible values for the mean, not the spread of individual scores.

items.s: A two-tailed test is more conservative than a one-tailed test at the same alpha.
items.why: The alpha is split across both tails, so the cutoff is farther from the mean.

items.s: Whether to use a one-tailed or two-tailed test
items.why: A one-tailed test is justified only when the direction was predicted in advance and a result in the other direction would be meaningless. Otherwise use two tails.
